analysis.one_liner: Repeals the fracking exemption from the Safe Drinking Water Act and requires disclosure of fracking chemicals.
analysis.headline: The bill to regulate fracking under the Safe Drinking Water Act and force disclosure of fracking chemicals died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would close the loophole that exempts hydraulic fracturing ("fracking") from the Safe Drinking Water Act, letting the EPA protect groundwater from fracking fluids the same way it regulates other underground injection [S2][S3]. It would also require fracking companies to disclose, before and after each operation, which chemicals they pump underground and in what volumes, and post that list publicly [S3]. Doctors and nurses could get the identity of trade-secret chemicals during a medical emergency without first signing paperwork [S2][S3]. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking operations and drink well water or rely on groundwater gain the most: the EPA could treat fracking fluids as underground injection and act on pollution risks, and chemical lists would be posted publicly rather than kept largely secret [S2][S3]. Emergency responders and treating physicians benefit because they could immediately learn what chemicals a patient was exposed to [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Safe Drinking Water Act exemption for hydraulic fracturing, giving the EPA authority to protect groundwater sources such as wells from pollution risks posed by fracking operations [S2][S3].

Requires operators to disclose chemicals intended for use before fracking starts and chemicals actually used within 30 days after it ends, including chemical identities, CAS numbers, safety data sheets, and volumes [S3].
Requires states or the EPA to post those chemical disclosures on a public website, so residents can see what was injected near them [S3].

Lets a treating physician or nurse get the identity of a trade-secret chemical during a medical emergency immediately, without a prior written statement of need or a confidentiality agreement [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that frack would bear new compliance costs: permits and oversight under the Safe Drinking Water Act's underground injection program, plus chemical disclosure and recordkeeping, and reduced ability to shield formulas as trade secrets. Those costs could be passed to consumers through slightly higher energy prices, and the industry argues the rules would slow drilling.

drawbacks.text: The bill subjects every fracking operation to federal underground injection permitting and chemical disclosure, which adds compliance costs and paperwork for operators and could slow drilling and raise energy costs [S3].

It narrows trade-secret protection: while proprietary formulas would not be posted publicly, operators must hand them over to states, the EPA, or medical staff on request in emergencies, which the industry views as a risk to confidential business information [S3].
The bill covers fracking related to geothermal production as well as oil and gas, so some non-fossil geothermal projects would also face the new permitting and disclosure requirements [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is groundwater protection and basic transparency about toxic chemicals pumped underground near homes and wells, with medical access in emergencies. The cost is real but ordinary: permitting and disclosure are standard regulatory burdens, and many states already run fracking disclosure programs. The main honest objection is that federal permitting could add delay and expense to drilling; the main honest defense is that fracking has been the only major form of underground injection exempt from the Safe Drinking Water Act, and the public currently cannot easily learn what is injected.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its environment subcommittee, and neither ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette introduced the bill on July 20, 2023, with 21 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
It accumulated 24 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in the House [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies that frack are better off: they keep their exemption from Safe Drinking Water Act permitting and face no federal chemical-disclosure mandate. The 25-member version of this bill has been introduced repeatedly over more than a decade and has never advanced; its death means groundwater near fracking sites remains regulated mainly by state rules rather than the EPA.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fracking companies that avoided new rules

sides.party_line_note: All 25 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and with Republicans holding the House majority the bill never moved past its subcommittee referral.

industries.note: The bill's core purpose is to end the industry's exemption from Safe Drinking Water Act underground injection permitting and to require public disclosure of the chemicals it pumps underground [S2][S3]. The industry's interest in keeping the exemption runs directly against the interest of residents who drink groundwater near drilling sites, and the industry's gain from the bill's death is continued freedom from federal permitting and disclosure.

industries.industry: Trade-secret chemical suppliers and service companies
industries.note: Suppliers of fracking fluid formulas would lose some trade-secret shielding: formulas would not be public, but they could be demanded by states, the EPA, or treating medical staff in emergencies [S3]. Their interest in secrecy is what the bill's disclosure provisions target, because residents and doctors currently cannot easily learn what chemicals were used.

The exemption repeal also covers underground injection from fracking related to geothermal production, so geothermal developers would face the same permitting and disclosure rules as oil and gas frackers [S3]. The effect on them is incidental rather than targeted.
